One language and the building of Babel (verses 1–4)

How quickly human beings forget even the most terrible judgments and return to their old sins!

The destruction caused by the flood was still fresh in their minds. They were descended from righteous Noah, and Noah himself was still alive.

Yet wickedness was already growing rapidly.

Nothing except the sanctifying grace of the Holy Spirit can remove the sinful desires of the human will and the corruption of the human heart.

God intended humanity to become many nations and populate the whole earth.

But most people came together in defiance of his will and against Noah's counsel.

They resolved to build a city and a tower so they would not have to separate.

Idolatry had begun, and Babel became one of its principal centers.

The builders encouraged one another, making each other bolder and more determined in evil.

Let us learn from this to encourage one another toward love and good works, as sinners encourage one another toward wickedness.

God confuses their language and scatters them (verses 5–9)

Scripture says the Lord came down to look at the city. This is language adapted to human understanding.

God is just and fair in everything he does against sin and sinners. He condemns no one without hearing the case.

The godly Eber was not among this rebellious company. He and his household belonged among God's children, and they did not join their souls to the gathering of those who lived without God.

The Lord allowed the builders to make considerable progress.

He intended the work from which they expected lasting honor to become an enduring disgrace.

God has wise and holy reasons for allowing enemies of his glory to succeed for a long time in their wicked schemes.

Consider both his wisdom and his mercy in the way he defeated their project.

His mercy appeared in making the punishment less severe than the offense deserved. God does not deal with us according to our sins.

His wisdom appeared in the sure means he chose to stop their work.

Once they could no longer understand one another, they could no longer help one another.

That would bring the building to an end.

God has many effective ways to defeat the schemes of proud people who oppose him. One of them is to divide them against one another.

However united and stubborn the builders had been, God was above them all. Who has ever hardened his heart against God and prospered?

Their language was confused.

We still suffer from that confusion. The trouble we take to learn other languages is part of the legacy of our ancestors' rebellion at Babel.

Perhaps even the unhappy disputes that arise from misunderstandings of words and arguments have their roots in that event.

The builders stopped working on the city.

The confusion of languages had made cooperation impossible. It also showed them that God's hand was against them.

It is wise to stop doing what we see God himself is opposing.

God can bring every scheme of Babel's builders to nothing. No wisdom or plan can prevail against the Lord.

The families separated according to their languages and went to the lands appointed for them.

Since that day, humanity has never gathered into one assembly as it did at Babel.

And it will not do so again until the great day when the Son of Man sits upon his glorious throne and all the nations gather before him.

The descendants of Shem (verses 10–26)

Here is a genealogy ending with Abram, the friend of God.

It leads us toward Christ, the promised Seed, who would descend from Abram.

Only names and ages are recorded. The Holy Spirit seems to hurry through these generations to reach Abram's story.

How little we know about people who lived before us, even in the very places where we now live!

We know just as little about many people living far away from us today.

We have enough to do in attending faithfully to the responsibilities God has given us.

As the earth became more populated, human lifespans began to shorten. This was the wise ordering of God's providence.

Terah's family leaves Ur and settles in Haran (verses 27–32)

Here begins the story of Abram, whose name is celebrated in both Testaments.

Even the descendants of Eber had become worshippers of false gods.

Those who, through grace, are heirs of the promised land should remember the land from which they came: their corrupt and sinful natural condition.

Abram had two brothers.

One was Nahor, from whose family both Isaac and Jacob would later take wives.

The other was Haran, Lot's father, who died before his own father.

Children cannot assume that they will outlive their parents.

Haran died in Ur, before the family had the blessing of leaving that idolatrous country.

We should therefore hurry to leave our natural condition of sin before death overtakes us in it.

Abram left Ur of the Chaldeans with his father Terah, his nephew Lot, and the rest of his family, in obedience to God's call.

This chapter leaves them partway between Ur and Canaan.

They settled there until Terah died.

Many people come as far as Haran but never reach Canaan.

They are not far from God's kingdom, yet they never enter it.

[Gen.11.1-Gen.11.4]
Chapter 11
Chapter Outline
One language in the world, The building of Babel. | (1-4) |
The confusion of tongues, The builders of Babel dispersed. | (5-9) |
The descendants of Shem. | (10-26) |
Terah, father of Abram, grandfather of Lot, they remove to Haran. | (27-32) |
Verses 1-4
How soon men forget the most tremendous judgments, and go back to their former crimes! Though the desolations of the deluge were before their eyes, though they sprang from the stock of righteous Noah, yet even during his life-time, wickedness increases exceedingly. Nothing but the sanctifying grace of the Holy Spirit can remove the sinful lusts of the human will, and the depravity of the human heart. God's purpose was, that mankind should form many nations, and people all lands. In contempt of the Divine will, and against the counsel of Noah, the bulk of mankind united to build a city and a tower to prevent their separating. Idolatry was begun, and Babel became one of its chief seats. They made one another more daring and resolute. Let us learn to provoke one another to love and to good works, as sinners stir up and encourage one another to wicked works.
[Gen.11.5-Gen.11.9]
Verses 5-9
Here is an expression after the manner of men; The Lord came down to see the city. God is just and fair in all he does against sin and sinners, and condemns none unheard. Pious Eber is not found among this ungodly crew; for he and his are called the children of God; their souls joined not themselves to the assembly of these children of men. God suffered them to go on some way, that the works of their hands, from which they promised themselves lasting honour, might turn to their lasting reproach. God has wise and holy ends, in allowing the enemies of his glory to carry on their wicked projects a great way, and to prosper long. Observe the wisdom and mercy of God, in the methods taken for defeating this undertaking. And the mercy of God in not making the penalty equal to the offence; for he deals not with us according to our sins. The wisdom of God, in fixing upon a sure way to stop these proceedings. If they could not understand one another, they could not help one another; this would take them off from their building. God has various means, and effectual ones, to baffle and defeat the projects of proud men that set themselves against him, and particularly he divides them among themselves. Notwithstanding their union and obstinacy God was above them; for who ever hardened his heart against him, and prospered? Their language was confounded. We all suffer by it to this day: in all the pains and trouble used to learn the languages we have occasion for, we suffer for the rebellion of our ancestors at Babel. Nay, and those unhappy disputes, which are strifes of words, and arise from misunderstanding one another's words, for aught we know, are owing to this confusion of tongues. They left off to build the city. The confusion of their tongues not only unfitted them for helping one another, but they saw the hand of the Lord gone out against them. It is wisdom to leave off that which we see God fights against. God is able to blast and bring to nought all the devices and designs of Babel-builders: there is no wisdom nor counsel against the Lord. The builders departed according to their families, and the tongue they spake, to the countries and places allotted to them. The children of men never did, nor ever will, come all together again, till the great day, when the Son of man shall sit upon the throne of his glory, and all nations shall be gathered before him.
[Gen.11.10-Gen.11.26]
Verses 10-26
Here is a genealogy, or list of names, ending in Abram, the friend of God, and thus leading towards Christ, the promised Seed, who was the son of Abram. Nothing is left upon record but their names and ages; the Holy Ghost seeming to hasten through them to the history of Abram. How little do we know of those that are gone before us in this world, even of those that lived in the same places where we live, as we likewise know little of those who now live in distant places! We have enough to do to mind our own work. When the earth began to be peopled, men's lives began to shorten; this was the wise disposal of Providence.
[Gen.11.27-Gen.11.32]
Verses 27-32
Here begins the story of Abram, whose name is famous in both Testaments. Even the children of Eber had become worshippers of false gods. Those who are through grace, heirs of the land of promise, ought to remember what was the land of their birth; what was their corrupt and sinful state by nature. Abram's brethren were, Nahor, out of whose family both Isaac and Jacob had their wives; and Haran, the father of Lot, who died before his father. Children cannot be sure that they shall outlive their parents. Haran died in Ur, before the happy removal of the family out of that idolatrous country. It concerns us to hasten out of our natural state, lest death surprise us in it. We here read of Abram's departure out of Ur of the Chaldees, with his father Terah, his nephew Lot, and the rest of his family, in obedience to the call of God. This chapter leaves them about mid-way between Ur and Canaan, where they dwelt till Terah's death. Many reach to Charran, and yet fall short of Canaan; they are not far from the kingdom of God, and yet never come thither.

God calls Abram and promises his blessing (verses 1–3)

God chose Abram out of the people around him, who worshipped idols.

His purpose was to preserve a people for himself, among whom the worship of the true God would continue until Christ came.

From this point on, Abram and his descendants become almost the only subject of the Bible's history.

God tested whether Abram loved him above everyone and everything else, and whether he would willingly leave all in order to follow him.

Abram's relatives and his father's household were a constant temptation. He could not stay among them without risking the spread of their idolatry into his own life.

Those who leave their sins and turn to God gain more than words can describe.

God's command to Abram resembles the gospel call. Natural affection must give way to divine grace when the two conflict.

We must forsake sin and everything that leads us into it, especially corrupting company.

God accompanied this command with great and precious promises. His commands come with promises for those who obey.

First, “I will make you a great nation.” God took Abram away from one people and promised to make him the head of another.

Second, “I will bless you.” Those who believe and obey are certain to inherit God's blessing.

Third, “I will make your name great.” God will certainly honor those who faithfully obey him.

Fourth, “You will be a blessing.” Godly people bring good to the nations and communities in which they live.

Fifth, “I will bless those who bless you, and curse the one who curses you.” God will not allow anyone who serves his people to lose by doing so.

Sixth, “In you all the families of the earth will be blessed.”

Jesus Christ is the world's greatest blessing—the greatest blessing it has ever received.

Every true blessing this world now enjoys or will ever enjoy comes through Abram and his descendants.

Through them we have received the Bible, the Savior, and the gospel.

They are the rootstock into which the Christian church has been grafted.

Abram leaves Haran (verses 4–5)

Abram believed that the blessing of the Almighty would more than compensate for everything he left behind.

God would supply all his needs and more than satisfy his deepest desires. Abram knew that disobedience could lead only to misery.

Believers who are justified by faith in Christ have peace with God.

They continue toward Canaan, neither discouraged by difficulties on the road nor drawn away by the pleasures they meet along it.

Those who begin the journey to heaven must persevere to the end.

Whatever we undertake in obedience to God's command and humble dependence on his providence will ultimately succeed and bring comfort.

Canaan was more than an outward possession, like other countries.

It was a picture of heaven. That is why the patriarchs valued it so deeply.

Abram worships God as he travels through Canaan (verses 6–9)

Abram found the land inhabited by Canaanites, who were troublesome neighbors.

He continued traveling from place to place.

Sometimes faithful people must live unsettled lives, moving repeatedly from one place to another.

Believers should remember that they are strangers and pilgrims in this world (Hebrews 11:8, 13–14).

Yet notice how much comfort Abram found in God.

He had little reason to enjoy fellowship with the Canaanites. But he found abundant delight in communion with the God who had brought him there and had not abandoned him.

We maintain fellowship with God through his word and prayer.

God makes himself and his favor known to his people gradually.

Earlier, he had promised to show Abram the land. Now he promised to give it to him.

As grace grows, comfort grows with it.

Abram seems to have understood the promise as a pledge of a better land, of which Canaan was a picture. He looked for a heavenly country (Hebrews 11:16).

As soon as Abram reached Canaan, though he was a stranger and traveler there, he established and maintained worship in his household.

He was concerned not only with the outward ceremonies of religion, such as offering sacrifices, but with sincerely seeking God and calling upon his name.

That is the spiritual sacrifice God delights to receive.

Abram also proclaimed the name of the Lord.

He taught his household and his neighbors to know the true God and his holy ways.

Family worship is not a recent invention. It is an ancient practice of God's people.

Abram was wealthy and responsible for a large household. He was unsettled and surrounded by enemies.

Yet wherever he pitched his tent, he built an altar.

Wherever we go, let us never leave our faith behind.

Abram's failure in Egypt (verses 10–20)

No place on earth is free from trials, and no human character is free from flaws.

Even Canaan, the glory of all lands, suffered famine.

And even Abram, the father of the faithful, showed unbelief and all the troubles it brings.

Perfect happiness and perfect purity belong only to heaven.

When Abram had to leave Canaan for a time, he went to Egypt rather than returning to the country he had left. He intended to remain only as long as necessary.

But in Egypt he disguised his relationship with Sarai.

He used misleading words and taught his wife and servants to do the same.

He concealed the truth so thoroughly that he effectively denied it. In doing so, he exposed both Sarai and the Egyptians to sin.

Abram was especially known for his faith. Yet he fell into this failure because he did not trust God's providence—even though God had already appeared to him twice.

If strong faith can be shaken like this, what will become of weak faith?

How often God must rescue us from danger and distress we bring upon ourselves through our own sin and foolishness!

Without his deliverance, we would be ruined. He does not deal with us as we deserve.

God's corrections are blessings when they stop us on a sinful path and bring us back to duty.

That includes the duty to return whatever we have wrongfully taken or kept.

Pharaoh was right to rebuke Abram: “What have you done?”

What an unworthy action for someone wise and godly!

When professing Christians behave unfairly, deceive others, or speak in a way that borders on lying, they must expect to be corrected.

They should even thank those who have the courage to tell them the truth.

Pharaoh treated Abram kindly when he sent him away.

Far from planning to kill Abram, as Abram had feared, Pharaoh took special care to protect him.

We often torment ourselves with fears that have no foundation. We are afraid when there is nothing to fear.

Pharaoh also ordered his servants not to harm Abram.

Those in authority must do more than avoid harming others themselves. They must restrain their servants and everyone under their care from doing harm too.

[Gen.12.1-Gen.12.3]
Chapter 12
Chapter Outline
God calls Abram, and blesses him with a promise of Christ. | (1-3) |
Abram departs from Haran. | (4-5) |
He journeys through Canaan, and worships God in that land. | (6-9) |
Abram is driven by a famine into Egypt, He feigns his wife to be his sister. | (10-20) |
Verses 1-3
God made choice of Abram, and singled him out from among his fellow-idolaters, that he might reserve a people for himself, among whom his true worship might be maintained till the coming of Christ. From henceforward Abram and his seed are almost the only subject of the history in the Bible. Abram was tried whether he loved God better than all, and whether he could willingly leave all to go with God. His kindred and his father's house were a constant temptation to him, he could not continue among them without danger of being infected by them. Those who leave their sins, and turn to God, will be unspeakable gainers by the change. The command God gave to Abram, is much the same with the gospel call, for natural affection must give way to Divine grace. Sin, and all the occasions of it, must be forsaken; particularly bad company. Here are many great and precious promises. All God's precepts are attended with promises to the obedient. 1. I will make of thee a great nation. When God took Abram from his own people, he promised to make him the head of another people. 2. I will bless thee. Obedient believers shall be sure to inherit the blessing. 3. I will make thy name great. The name of obedient believers shall certainly be made great. 4. Thou shalt be a blessing. Good men are the blessings of their country. 5. I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee. God will take care that none are losers, by any service done for his people. 6. In thee shall all the families of the earth be blessed. Jesus Christ is the great blessing of the world, the greatest that ever the world possessed. All the true blessedness the world is now, or ever shall be possessed of, is owing to Abram and his posterity. Through them we have a Bible, a Saviour, and a gospel. They are the stock on which the Christian church is grafted.
[Gen.12.4-Gen.12.5]
Verses 4-5
Abram believed that the blessing of the Almighty would make up for all he could lose or leave behind, supply all his wants, and answer and exceed all his desires; and he knew that nothing but misery would follow disobedience. Such believers, being justified by faith in Christ, have peace with God. They hold on their way to Canaan. They are not discouraged by the difficulties in their way, nor drawn aside by the delights they meet with. Those who set out for heaven must persevere to the end. What we undertake, in obedience to God's command, and in humble attendance on his providence, will certainly succeed, and end with comfort at last. Canaan was not, as other lands, a mere outward possession, but a type of heaven, and in this respect the patriarchs so earnestly prized it.
[Gen.12.6-Gen.12.9]
Verses 6-9
Abram found the country peopled by Canaanites, who were bad neighbours. He journeyed, going on still. Sometimes it is the lot of good men to be unsettled, and often to remove into various states. Believers must look on themselves as strangers and sojourners in this world, [Heb.11.8] He 11:8, [Heb.13.14] 13, 14. But observe how much comfort Abram had in God. When he could have little satisfaction in converse with the Canaanites whom he found there, he had abundance of pleasure in communion with that God, who brought him thither, and did not leave him. Communion with God is kept up by the word and by prayer. God reveals himself and his favours to his people by degrees; before, he had promised to show Abram this land, now, to give it to him: as grace is growing, so is comfort. It should seem, Abram understood it also as a grant of a better land, of which this was a type; for he looked for a heavenly country, [Heb.11.16] He 11:16. As soon as Abram was got to Canaan, though he was but a stranger and sojourner there, yet he set up, and kept up, the worship of God in his family. He not only minded the ceremonial part of religion, the offering of sacrifice; but he made conscience of seeking his God, and calling on his name; that spiritual sacrifice with which God is well pleased. He preached concerning the name of the Lord; he taught his family and neighbours the knowledge of the true God, and his holy religion. The way of family worship is a good old way, no new thing, but the ancient usage of the saints. Abram was rich, and had a numerous family, was now unsettled, and in the midst of enemies; yet, wherever he pitched his tent, he built an altar: wherever we go, let us not fail to take our religion along with us.
[Gen.12.10-Gen.12.20]
Verses 10-20
There is no state on earth free from trials, nor any character free from blemishes. There was famine in Canaan, the glory of all lands, and unbelief, with the evils it ever brings, in Abram the father of the faithful. Perfect happiness and perfect purity dwell only in heaven. Abram, when he must for a time quit Canaan, goes to Egypt, that he might not seem to look back, and meaning to tarry there no longer than needful. There Abram dissembled his relation to Sarai, equivocated, and taught his wife and his attendants to do so too. He concealed a truth, so as in effect to deny it, and exposed thereby both his wife and the Egyptians to sin. The grace Abram was most noted for, was faith; yet he thus fell through unbelief and distrust of the Divine providence, even after God had appeared to him twice. Alas, what will become of weak faith, when strong faith is thus shaken! If God did not deliver us, many a time, out of straits and distresses which we bring ourselves into, by our own sin and folly, we should be ruined. He deals not with us according to our deserts. Those are happy chastisements that hinder us in a sinful way, and bring us to our duty, particularly to the duty of restoring what we have wrongfully taken or kept. Pharaoh's reproof of Abram was very just: What is this that thou hast done? How unbecoming a wise and good man! If those who profess religion, do that which is unfair and deceptive, especially if they say that which borders upon a lie, they must expect to hear of it; and they have reason to thank those who will tell them of it. The sending away was kind. Pharaoh was so far from any design to kill Abram, as he feared, that he took particular care of him. We often perplex ourselves with fears which are altogether groundless. Many a time we fear where no fear is. Pharaoh charged his men not to hurt Abram in any thing. It is not enough for those in authority, that they do not hurt themselves; they must keep their servants and those about them from doing hurt.

Abram returns to Bethel (verses 1–4)

Abram was exceedingly rich.

The Hebrew expression means that he was very heavy with wealth. Riches can indeed become a heavy burden.

Those who are determined to become rich load themselves down with what Scripture calls thick clay (Habakkuk 2:6).

Getting wealth brings the burden of anxiety; keeping it brings fear; using it brings temptation; misusing it brings guilt; losing it brings sorrow.

And at the end, we must give an account of what we have done with it.

Yet God's providence sometimes makes godly people wealthy.

God's blessing made Abram rich without bringing sorrow with it (Proverbs 10:22).

It is difficult for a rich person to enter heaven. But in some cases it is possible (Mark 10:23–24).

When outward prosperity is used wisely, it can adorn a godly life and give us more opportunities to do good.

Abram returned to Bethel.

His former altar was gone, so he could not offer sacrifices there. But he still called on the name of the Lord.

You are as likely to find a living person who never breathes as a true child of God who never prays.

Abram makes peace with Lot (verses 5–9)

Riches provide endless occasions for quarrels. They are among the things people fight about most often.

They also stir up the spirit of conflict itself by making people proud and greedy.

“Mine” and “yours” have caused countless disputes.

Poverty, work, deprivation, and wandering had not separated Abram from Lot. But wealth did.

Bad servants can cause tremendous trouble in families and among neighbors through pride, anger, lies, slander, and gossip.

The quarrel was especially damaging because the Canaanites and Perizzites lived in the land.

When those who profess faith quarrel, they bring disgrace on religion and give God's enemies an excuse to blaspheme.

It is best to preserve peace before it is broken.

But once a quarrel has begun, the next best thing is to put out the fire as quickly as possible.

Abram took the initiative, although he was the older man and held the greater position.

His calm spirit enabled him to control his anger and turn away wrath with a gentle answer.

Those who want peace must never answer insults with more insults.

Abram also showed humility. He was willing to plead for peace even with someone in a lower position than himself.

Whatever others may choose, God's people must be people of peace.

Abram gave a powerful reason for reconciliation: the people of the world may fight over trifles, but we who know better things and hope for a better country should not quarrel.

Christians should be especially careful to avoid disputes.

Many people claim to love peace but do nothing to make it happen. Abram was different.

If God himself stoops to plead with us to be reconciled to him, surely we can plead with one another.

Although God had promised the land to Abram's descendants, Abram offered Lot an equal or even better portion.

Lot did not have the same claim, but Abram would not use God's promise as an excuse to treat a relative harshly.

It is noble to give way for the sake of peace.

Lot chooses the land near Sodom (verses 10–13)

Abram gave Lot the choice, and Lot immediately accepted it.

Selfishness and strong desire often make people discourteous.

Lot looked at the land's fertility and assumed he would surely prosper in such a fruitful place.

But how did his choice turn out?

When people choose their relationships, work, homes, or places to settle mainly according to bodily desire, the attraction of what they see, or pride, they cannot expect God's presence and blessing.

They are often disappointed even in the thing they most wanted.

One principle should govern every choice: what is best for our souls is best for us.

Lot gave little thought to the character of the people who lived nearby.

Sodom's inhabitants were bold and unashamed in their sin.

The city's wickedness included pride, abundance of food, and an excess of idleness (Ezekiel 16:49).

God often allows great plenty to belong to great sinners.

It has frequently been the painful experience of godly people to live among wicked neighbors.

That pain is even greater when, as with Lot, they have brought the situation upon themselves through a poor choice.

God renews his promise to Abram (verses 14–18)

Those whose spirits are calm, rather than disturbed by angry passions, are best prepared to receive visits of God's grace.

God more than makes up for the outward advantages we give up to preserve peace with our neighbors by giving us spiritual peace.

Even when our relatives separate from us, God does not leave us.

Notice how God now comforted and enriched Abram through his promises.

He promised two things: a good land and many descendants to enjoy it.

What faith sees is richer and more beautiful than anything our eyes can see around us.

God told Abram to walk throughout the land.

He was not to imagine that he could settle there permanently. Rather, he would remain a pilgrim, moving toward a better Canaan.

Abram built an altar as a sign of his thankfulness.

When God meets us with gracious promises, he expects us to respond with humble praise.

When outward circumstances are difficult, believers find great benefit in meditating on the glorious inheritance the Lord has prepared for them at the end.

Chapter 13
Chapter Outline
Abram returns out of Egypt with great riches. | (1-4) |
Strife between the herdsmen of Abram and Lot. Abram gives Lot his choice of the country. | (5-9) |
Lot chooses to dwell at Sodom. | (10-13) |
God renews his promise to Abram, who removes to Hebron. | (14-18) |
Verses 1-4
Abram was very rich: he was very heavy, so the Hebrew word is; for riches are a burden; and they that will be rich, do but load themselves with thick clay, [Hab.2.6] Ha 2:6. There is a burden of care in getting riches, fear in keeping them, temptation in using them, guilt in abusing them, sorrow in losing them, and a burden of account at last to be given up about them. Yet God in his providence sometimes makes good men rich men, and thus God's blessing made Abram rich without sorrow, [Prov.10.22] Pr 10:22. Though it is hard for a rich man to get to heaven, yet in some cases it may be, [Mark.10.23] Mr 10:23, [Mark.10.24] 24. Nay, outward prosperity, if well managed, is an ornament to piety, and an opportunity for doing more good. Abram removed to Bethel. His altar was gone, so that he could not offer sacrifice; but he called on the name of the Lord. You may as soon find a living man without breath as one of God's people without prayer.
[Gen.13.5-Gen.13.9]
Verses 5-9
Riches not only afford matter for strife, and are the things most commonly striven about; but they also stir up a spirit of contention, by making people proud and covetous. Mine and thine are the great make-bates of the world. Poverty and labour, wants and wanderings, could not separate Abram and Lot; but riches did so. Bad servants often make a great deal of mischief in families and among neighbours, by their pride and passion, lying, slandering, and talebearing. What made the quarrel worse was, that the Canaanite and the Perizzite dwelt then in the land. The quarrels of professors are the reproach of religion, and give occasion to the enemies of the Lord to blaspheme. It is best to keep the peace, that it be not broken; but the next best is, if differences do happen, with all speed to quench the fire that is broken out. The attempt to stay this strife was made by Abram, although he was the elder and the greater man. Abraham welcomes the visitors (verses 1–8)

Abraham was ready to welcome any tired traveler who came his way.

There were no inns like those we have today.

As Abraham sat there, he saw three men approaching.

They were three heavenly beings appearing in human bodies.

Some believe all three were created angels. Others believe one of them was the Son of God, the Angel of the covenant.

Washing guests' feet was a common act of hospitality in hot countries where people wore sandals.

We should not neglect to welcome strangers. In doing so, some have welcomed angels without knowing it (Hebrews 13:2).

More than that, we welcome the Lord of angels himself whenever we show kindness for his sake to the least of his brothers and sisters.

Cheerful and thoughtful kindness is one of the finest ornaments of a godly life.

Our gracious and humble Lord no longer visits us personally in the way he visited Abraham.

Yet through his Spirit he still stands at the door and knocks.

When we are willing to open, he graciously enters and provides a rich feast of comfort, which we share with him (Revelation 3:20).

Sarah's unbelief is corrected (verses 9–15)

The visitors asked where Sarah was.

Abraham replied, “In the tent.”

She was close by, in the right place, attending to her household duties.

There is nothing to gain from wandering around aimlessly.

Those who are faithfully carrying out their duties are most likely to receive comfort from God and his promises (Luke 2:8).

We are often slow to believe, and we need to hear the same truth repeatedly.

Other people may receive blessings through God's ordinary providence.

Believers receive those same blessings through his promises, which make them sweeter and more certain.

Abraham's spiritual descendants owe their life, joy, hope, and everything else to God's promise.

Sarah thought the news of a son too wonderful to be true.

She laughed because she could not yet bring herself to believe it.

At first we might not see any difference between Sarah's laughter and Abraham's laughter in Genesis 17:17.

But God, who searches the heart, saw that her laughter arose from unbelief, while his arose from faith.

Sarah then denied that she had laughed.

One sin often leads to another. When we question God's truth, we are less likely to speak the truth ourselves.

Yet the Lord rebukes, convicts, silences, and brings to repentance those whom he loves when they sin before him.

God tells Abraham about Sodom (verses 16–22)

Two of the visitors, understood to be created angels, went toward Sodom.

The third, called Jehovah throughout this account, remained with Abraham.

He chose not to hide from Abraham what he intended to do.

God sometimes shows great patience toward sinners.

They may wrongly conclude that he neither notices nor cares about what they do.

But when the day of his judgment comes, he will look toward them.

God told Abraham what he intended to do, giving him an opportunity to intercede and showing him the justice of his actions.

Abraham's character shines especially in the care he took over his family.

He not only prayed with them but taught and governed them conscientiously.

Those who expect the blessings of a godly family must also fulfill the duties of a godly family.

Abraham did not fill his household's minds with doubtful controversies.

He taught them to worship God sincerely and seriously, and to deal honestly with everyone.

How few households could receive such praise today!

How little care is often taken to teach those under our responsibility the foundations of true religion.

Do we watch, week after week, to see whether they are making progress or falling behind?

Abraham intercedes for Sodom (verses 23–33)

Here we find the first solemn prayer recorded in Scripture.

Abraham prayed that Sodom might be spared if only a few righteous people could be found there.

We should learn from him how deeply to care for sinners and how earnestly to pray for them.

The fervent prayer of a righteous person can accomplish much.

Abraham did not obtain what he requested for the whole city.

Yet Lot was delivered in a miraculous way.

Let this encourage us to pray earnestly for God's blessing upon our families, friends, and neighborhoods.

But we must do more than pray. We must also live as Abraham did.

Abraham knew that the Judge of all the earth would do what was right.

He did not argue that the wicked deserved to be spared on their own account.

Nor did he suggest that destroying them would be unjust or excessively severe.

He pleaded for the sake of the righteous people who might still be among them.

Only righteousness can serve as a plea before God.

How, then, did Christ intercede for transgressors?

Not by criticizing God's law or offering excuses that minimize human guilt.

He pleaded his own obedience, even to death.

In Sodom, Lot remained pure.

He grieved over the city's wickedness and testified against it.

Yet later, while alone in the mountains, believing himself safely beyond temptation, he fell into a shameful sin.

Whoever thinks he is standing high and securely must be careful not to fall.

Notice also the danger of drunkenness.

People often do things while drunk that would horrify them to contemplate when sober.

There is also danger in temptations that come from relatives and friends.

These are people we love and respect, and from whom we expect kindness.

Dishonest schemes do not prosper. They place both ourselves and others in danger.

Yet if we have done wrong without knowing it, our ignorance will not excuse us if we continue to do wrong after we learn the truth.

His actions brought suffering upon other people and exposed both himself and Sarah to justified rebuke.

Yet he still tried to excuse himself.

Those who remain proud and refuse to repent must never use God's grace as an excuse for continuing to sin.

Sometimes we discover reverence for God in the very people among whom we least expected to find it.
